answer.answer:
**Summary**

Adopting a robotic process is not only a machine purchase: the delivery model, business model and work culture have to move with it, and that change is recorded as a genuine directional requirement rather than a correlation. In practice this means bringing the party that will actually fabricate and assemble into design early, tightening organisational coupling so that a technically interdependent system sits inside one accountable entity, committing to prefabrication and standardised components upstream of the robot, and funding training and robot safety compliance before the first collaborative task. What you get back is error reduction and, on geometrically complex work, real productivity and cost gains. Watch that the delivery-model change is the thinnest-evidenced link in the chain: it rests on a single cited path into robotic assembly, and the deployed case in front of me does not record it as active.

**Detailed answer**

**The direct requirement.** Robotic assembly (PR4) depends on delivery/business model/work culture (RI12), on the grounds that robotics adoption in precast production rests on the environmental and organisational context, with peer-reviewed evidence (DEP61) [1]. RI12 carries exactly two inbound and no outbound dependency edges [2], the second being AT8 depending on RI12, because adopting digital fabrication at industrialised scale depends on adapted business models (DEP81, peer-reviewed) [2]. So the delivery model is a receiving condition, not a lever that produces other capabilities. RI12 is activated in 16 of the 50 coded cases [2], so this is a common but not universal reconfiguration.

**What specifically changes in the delivery arrangement.** Contracting has to pull production knowledge forward: integrating manufacturing and assembly knowledge into design requires the delivering production party, manufacturer, fabricator or contractor, to be involved in the early design phase, and a delivery method that involves participants in early design should be selected (DEP22, CO11 enables PR2) [2]. The same early involvement improves design management and increases digital fabrication adoption (DEP65) [2], and technically interdependent systems require tighter organisational coupling such as a single firm (DEP35, AT12 has precondition CO10) [2], with interdisciplinary team integration linking actors to integrated design-DFAB processes (DEP85) [2].

**Upstream production and workforce commitments.** Automated overhead delivery and assembly requires extensive prefabrication and unification of materials (DEP55) [2], and Japanese automated erection systems rely on standardised prefabricated components (DEP88) [2]. On the labour side, human-robot collaboration is contingent on a skilled workforce and so depends on addressing workforce training (DEP34) [2], and it depends on compliance with robot safety standards (DEP45, standards evidence) [2].

**What the change buys.** Robotic and factory assembly reduces errors (DEP21) [2], and productivity is higher when the robotic method is used for geometrically complex walls (DEP95) [2].

**Deployed evidence.** The case in front of me is RP18, adopted to address quality and labor, performing steelwork and surface treatment on the structural core as a mobile robot on site, outdoors, at technology readiness level 7 [3]; it activates the robot arm (RE2), path planning (PR12) and human-robot collaboration (CO6), and is recorded in the census as census_RXM4-1 [4]. Notably, RI12 is not among RP18's listed activations, so this deployment does not evidence the delivery-model change itself. No firm is named for RP18; the one retrieved record that names a developer is census_RXH3-4, developed by Firm_144 as a census record of RP8 [4], performing inspection and material handling on the facade at techn [5]
